q680: God is described as a parent who is 'slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy' (Psalm 103:8). He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). In the same way, toddlers need patience because they are small. The Bible also offers grace to parents. 'His compassions fail not. They are new every morning' (Lamentations 3:22-23). Repairing after a mistake models the gospel: we are honest about wrongdoing and we receive forgiveness. James says, 'Confess your faults one to another' (James 5:16), and that includes our children. Jesus took children in His arms (Mark 10:16). Gentle closeness is His way.
q681: God designed children to calm down by borrowing a calm adult's nervous system. This is called co-regulation. When a parent stays near and steady, the child's brain gradually learns to settle itself. Shouting usually adds fear, which can stop the behaviour but does not build the child's own brakes. Repair after conflict also teaches children that relationships survive mistakes, which research links with secure attachment. Parents need rest and support to stay regulated, because we can only give calm we have received.
q682: Lamentations 3:22-23|It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning
q686: Fatima still shouts sometimes, especially when she is unwell or has slept badly. But it happens far less. Ayaan's tantrums have shortened as he has grown and as she stays calm. When she does lose her temper, she kneels down and says sorry, and Ayaan now sometimes says, 'Sorry Ammi,' too. Her mother-in-law still criticises, but Fatima feels steadier inside.
q687: Calm closeness and honest repair teach children more than shouting, and parents need grace too.
q688: Little children have big feelings. Grown-ups can stay calm, give hugs and say sorry when they get it wrong.
q689: Kavitha and the kitchen with too many voices
q690: Kavitha, 30, an architect in Coimbatore, living in a joint family
q691: When Kavitha married Suresh, she moved into his family home with his parents, his younger brother and his brother's wife. She loved Suresh, but the house felt crowded. Her mother-in-law corrected how she cooked, how she dressed and how she spent money. Kavitha worked full-time as an architect but was still expected to cook dinner every night. When she raised concerns, Suresh said, 'Please adjust, Amma is old.' Kavitha began to resent both her mother-in-law and her husband. She cried in the bathroom and ate dinner quietly. Once, after a comment about her not yet having children, she snapped back and the whole family went silent. She felt like an outsider in her own home.
q692: In many joint families, unspoken expectations and roles are passed down for generations. Kavitha's mother-in-law had herself been treated harshly as a young bride, and some of her criticism came from that old pattern. Suresh was caught in a triangle between his mother and his wife, and his avoidance came from fear of disrespecting his parents. Kavitha's nervous system was constantly on alert, never fully relaxed at home, which research suggests can lead to exhaustion and irritability. Underneath her anger was loneliness and a longing to be valued. Without clear, respectful communication, resentment grew on all sides.
q693: During a church marriage retreat, Suresh heard a talk about leaving and cleaving. He realised his first loyalty after marriage was to Kavitha. That night he apologised for not standing beside her. They began to plan together how to honour his parents while protecting their marriage.
q694: Suresh and Kavitha agreed to discuss concerns privately first, then speak as a team
q695: Used DEAR MAN to ask respectfully for shared cooking duties
q696: Set a gentle boundary about questions on having children
q697: Created one evening a week for just the two of them
q698: Kavitha practised naming her feelings before reacting
q699: Genesis says, 'Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife' (Genesis 2:24). Leaving does not mean abandoning parents, but it does mean a new primary loyalty. The Bible also commands, 'Honour thy father and thy mother' (Exodus 20:12). Both are true. Ruth and Naomi show how deep love can grow between in-laws when there is loyalty and kindness (Ruth 1:16). Scripture asks us to speak 'the truth in love' (Ephesians 4:15), and to 'live peaceably with all men' as much as possible (Romans 12:18). Respectful honesty honours everyone.
q700: God designed us to feel safe and loved in our homes. When a couple acts as a team, the nervous systems of both partners settle. Clear boundaries reduce constant conflict, which lowers stress for the whole family. Research suggests that respectful, assertive communication builds more lasting peace than either silent compliance or angry outbursts. When people feel heard, even difficult conversations can bring families closer rather than pulling them apart.
q701: Romans 12:18|If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men
q705: Things did not become perfect. Her mother-in-law still comments on the cooking, and there are tense days. But Suresh now speaks up gently, and Kavitha feels less alone. After a few months, the family agreed on shared cooking days. Recently her mother-in-law taught her a family recipe, and they laughed together in the kitchen for the first time. They are now looking at renting a flat nearby.
q706: In joint families, a united couple and respectful honesty create space for peace with in-laws.
q707: When families live together, it can be hard. Talking kindly and working as a team helps everyone feel loved.
q708: Siddharth and the game that ate his nights
q709: Siddharth, 23, a final-year commerce student in Jaipur
q710: Siddharth started gaming to relax after failing his first attempt at a competitive exam. Soon he was playing eight to ten hours a day. He would stay up until four, sleep through classes and skip meals. He told his parents he was studying. His online team relied on him, and he felt more important there than anywhere else. When his father found out, there was a huge fight, and Siddharth broke his phone in anger. He felt ashamed, but the next night he was back online on his laptop. His friends from college had moved on to jobs and he had stopped answering their messages. He told his cousin, 'When I am not playing, I feel like nothing.'
q711: Games are designed to give constant rewards, progress and a sense of mastery. For Siddharth, gaming gave him what real life seemed to have taken away: achievement, belonging and escape from shame. After his exam failure, he felt like a disappointment to his family. The game numbed that pain. Research suggests that compulsive gaming can be linked with low mood, anxiety and lack of purpose, and that the brain's reward system can become less sensitive to everyday pleasures. Sleep loss made his mood worse, which made him game more. The game was not just a bad habit. It was a hiding place for a wounded sense of worth.
q712: His cousin, who had beaten a similar habit, told Siddharth, 'The game is not your enemy. It is telling you what you are hungry for.' Siddharth realised he was hungry for purpose and respect. He agreed to see a counsellor who works with gaming problems.
q713: Met weekly with a counsellor experienced in gaming addiction
q714: Uninstalled the main game and moved his laptop out of his bedroom
q715: Made if-then plans for evenings when the urge was strongest
q716: Started a part-time job tutoring younger students
q717: Rejoined a cricket group on weekends
q718: Practised urge surfing when he felt restless
q719: Scripture warns that what we repeatedly give ourselves to can master us: 'of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage' (2 Peter 2:19). But the Bible also speaks to our deep hunger for meaning. God created humans to work and steward the earth (Genesis 2:15). Paul writes, 'whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord' (Colossians 3:23). Jesus offers not just freedom from but freedom to: 'I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly' (John 10:10). Our worth is not in winning or performing but in being loved by God.
q720: God made us to grow through effort and real-world rewards. When our lives lack purpose and connection, the brain seeks quick substitutes. Research suggests that reducing exposure to highly rewarding triggers while adding meaningful activities helps the reward system recalibrate. Physical activity, friendships and work that helps others release natural rewards that build lasting wellbeing. If-then plans let the brain prepare for urges in advance. Over time, healthy pathways strengthen and old cravings fade, though they may return under stress.
q721: John 10:10|I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly
q725: Siddharth had two serious relapses in the first six months, both after stressful exam results. Each time, he told his counsellor and started again. Now he plays occasionally with a strict time limit on weekends. He is preparing for his exam again with a study group. He still feels the pull when he is lonely, but he also feels proud of the students he tutors.
q726: Compulsive habits often hide unmet hungers, and healing comes when we fill those hungers with real purpose and connection.
q727: Games can be fun, but they cannot fill our hearts. Friends, helping others and God give us real joy.
q728: Nikhil and the empty desk at the office
q729: Nikhil, 27, a data entry analyst in Gurugram, single
q730: Nikhil had moved to Gurugram for a corporate job that sounded impressive to his relatives back home in Bihar. In reality, he spent nine hours a day copying numbers between spreadsheets. No one noticed his work. His manager only spoke to him when something went wrong. Most evenings he came back to a small rented room, ate takeaway and opened his laptop. Within an hour he would be watching pornography, sometimes for hours. Afterwards he felt disgusted with himself and promised God it would be the last time. He deleted apps, installed blockers, fasted and memorised verses. Each time he lasted a few days and then fell again. He began to believe he was simply a weak and dirty person, and he stopped going to church.
q731: Nikhil's behaviour was not random. When he started tracking what happened before each episode, a clear pattern appeared. It was worst on days when his work felt pointless and invisible. The fantasies he was drawn to were often about being wanted and powerful, the opposite of how he felt at his desk. Pornography offered a quick hit of excitement and significance to a man starving for meaning. Research suggests that compulsive habits often grow where life feels flat and purposeless. His white-knuckle efforts failed because they only fought the behaviour and never touched the hunger underneath. Shame then made him hide more, which deepened the loneliness.
q732: A men's group leader asked him, 'What was your day like before the last time?' Nikhil said, 'Useless.' The leader said, 'Then maybe the problem is not only lust. Maybe it is futility.' For the first time, Nikhil felt curious about his behaviour instead of only hating himself.
q733: Kept a 'before' log noting his mood and day before each urge
q734: Confessed honestly to a trusted older friend in his church men's group
q735: Started volunteering on Saturdays teaching computer skills to children in a nearby community centre
q736: Began exploring a career change into data analysis, which he found meaningful
q737: Called his accountability partner when evenings felt empty
q738: Saw a Christian counsellor to work on shame and purpose
q739: Ecclesiastes is honest about futility: 'all is vanity and vexation of spirit' (Ecclesiastes 1:14). Life without purpose feels empty, and empty hearts reach for false fillers. God created us to work with meaning, tending and keeping His world (Genesis 2:15). Paul says we are 'his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Ephesians 2:10). Freedom is not only saying no to sin but saying yes to the good God has prepared. Confession brings healing: 'Confess your faults one to another... that ye may be healed' (James 5:16). God's mercy meets us not when we are clean but while we are still struggling (Romans 5:8).
q740: God designed us with a deep need for meaning and contribution. When work and life feel purposeless, the brain's reward system seeks intensity elsewhere. Curiosity about our behaviour engages the thinking brain and quiets shame, which research suggests is a stronger engine of compulsion than desire alone. Purposeful activity, service and genuine connection give the brain healthy rewards and a sense of significance. Honest confession breaks the isolation that feeds secret habits. As life gains purpose, the pull of false comfort weakens naturally.
q741: Ephesians 2:10|For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works
q745: Nikhil did not become instantly free. He slipped several times in the first year, often on difficult work days. But instead of hiding, he called his friend and talked about what happened. The episodes became much less frequent. After a year he moved into a data analysis role he enjoys. He still has hard evenings, but he now knows what they are telling him.
q746: Unwanted sexual behaviour often points to a deeper hunger, and pursuing real purpose brings more freedom than fighting alone.
q747: Sometimes we do wrong things because we feel empty inside. When we find good things to do, God helps us feel full.
